questions.text:
Consider the given system of linear equations for variables [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex], where [latex]k[/latex] is a real-valued constant. Which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?

[latex]x + k y = 1[/latex]
[latex]k x + y = -1[/latex]
questions.solution:
[latex]\begin{cases}x+ky=1\\kx+y=-1\end{cases}[/latex], with determinant [latex]\Delta=1-k^2[/latex].

No solution requires [latex]\Delta=0[/latex] (i.e. [latex]k=\pm1[/latex]) and the two equations to actually be inconsistent (parallel but not identical lines):
- [latex]k=1[/latex]: equations become [latex]x+y=1[/latex] and [latex]x+y=-1[/latex] — parallel, contradictory → no solution.
- [latex]k=-1[/latex]: equations become [latex]x-y=1[/latex] and [latex]-x+y=-1[/latex], which is just the first equation multiplied by [latex]-1[/latex] — the same line → infinitely many solutions, not "no solution."

So there is exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] (namely [latex]k=1[/latex]) giving no solution, and exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] (namely [latex]k=-1[/latex]) giving infinitely many solutions. For every other [latex]k[/latex] (i.e. [latex]k\ne\pm1[/latex]), [latex]\Delta\ne0[/latex] and there's a unique solution — but that happens for infinitely many values of [latex]k[/latex], not just one, so the "exactly one k gives a unique solution" claim is false.

Answer: Exactly one k gives no solution; and exactly one k gives infinitely many solutions.

Click here for detail solution
options: There is exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] for which the above system of equations has no solution.
There exist an infinite number of values of [latex]k[/latex] for which the system of equations has no solution.
There exists exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] for which the system of equations has exactly one solution.
There exists exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] for which the system of equations has an infinite number of solutions.

questions.text: Let [latex]A[/latex]  be an [latex] n \times n[/latex]  matrix over the set of all real numbers [latex]R[/latex]. Let [latex]B[/latex]  be a matrix obtained from [latex]A[/latex] by swapping two rows. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Swapping two rows changes the sign of the determinant: [latex]\det B=-\det A[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- So [latex]\det A\ne0\Rightarrow\det B\ne0[/latex]: B is invertible [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{bmatrix}[/latex] is symmetric, but [latex]B=\begin{bmatrix}2&3\\1&2\end{bmatrix}[/latex] is not [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}[/latex] has trace 0, but [latex]B=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}[/latex] has trace 1 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1 and 2

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: The determinant of [latex]B[/latex] is the negative of the determinant of [latex]A[/latex]
If [latex]A[/latex] is invertible, then [latex]B[/latex] is also invertible
If [latex]A[/latex] is symmetric, then [latex]B[/latex] is also symmetric
If the trace of [latex]A[/latex] is zero, then the trace of [latex]B[/latex] is also zero

questions.text: Let [latex] x [/latex] and [latex] y [/latex] be random variables, not necessarily independent, that take real values in the interval [latex] [0,1] [/latex]. Let [latex] z=x y [/latex] and let the mean values of [latex] x, y, z [/latex] be [latex] \bar{x}, \bar{y}, \bar{z} [/latex], respectively. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.solution:
Since [latex]0\le y\le1[/latex], we always have [latex]z=xy\le x[/latex]. Taking means: [latex]\bar z\le\bar x[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] always TRUE.

Others depend on how x and y are related:
- [latex]y=x[/latex] uniform on [0, 1]: [latex]\bar z=E[x^2]=\frac13 \gt \frac14=\bar x\bar y[/latex] (so = and [latex]\le[/latex] fail).
- [latex]y=1-x[/latex]: [latex]\bar z=\frac12-\frac13=\frac16 \lt \frac14[/latex] (so [latex]\ge[/latex] fails).

Answer: [latex]\bar z\le\bar x[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: [latex] \bar{z}=\bar{x} \bar{y} [/latex]
[latex]  \bar{z} \leq \bar{x} \bar{y} [/latex]
[latex] \bar{z} \geq \bar{x} \bar{y} [/latex]
[latex] \bar{z} \leq \bar{x} [/latex]

questions.text:
Let [latex] f(x) [/latex] be a continuous function from [latex] \mathbb{R} [/latex] to [latex] \mathbb{R} [/latex] such that
[latex] f(x)=1-f(2-x) [/latex]
Which one of the following options is the CORRECT value of [latex] \int_0^2 f(x) d x [/latex] ?
questions.solution:
Let [latex]I=\int_0^2 f(x)\,dx[/latex]. Substituting [latex]x\to2-x[/latex] gives [latex]I=\int_0^2 f(2-x)\,dx[/latex].

Adding both: [latex]2I=\int_0^2\big(f(x)+f(2-x)\big)dx=\int_0^2 1\,dx=2[/latex]

[latex]I=1[/latex]

Answer: 1

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: [latex] 0  [/latex]
[latex] 1  [/latex]
[latex] 2  [/latex]
[latex] -1  [/latex]

questions.text: Let [latex] A [/latex] be any [latex] n \times m [/latex] matrix, where [latex] m > n [/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE about the system of linear equations [latex] A x=0 [/latex] ?
questions.solution:
[latex]rank(A)\le n \lt m[/latex], so the solution space has dimension [latex]m-rank(A)\ge m-n[/latex].

- At least [latex]m-n[/latex] linearly independent solutions [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- "[latex]m-n[/latex] vectors span every solution" fails when the dimension is larger, e.g. A = zero matrix (dimension m) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- [latex]A=[1\;\;1][/latex] ([latex]n=1,m=2[/latex]): solutions are [latex]t(1,-1)[/latex]; no non-zero solution has a zero entry, though [latex]m-n=1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{bmatrix}[/latex]: solutions [latex](0,0,t)[/latex] have only 1 non-zero variable [latex]\lt n=2[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: There exist at least [latex]m-n[/latex] linearly independent solutions

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: There exist at least [latex] m-n [/latex] linearly independent solutions to this system
There exist [latex] m-n [/latex] linearly independent vectors such that every solution is a linear combination of these vectors
There exists a non-zero solution in which at least [latex] m-n [/latex] variables are 0
There exists a solution in which at least [latex] n [/latex] variables are non-zero
